name: Emideltide (DSIP)

track.title: Lab & animal
track.line: Rabbit, rat and cat studies since the 1970s

track.title: Phase I
track.line: No formal Phase I trial found

track.title: FDA approval
track.line: Not approved; FDA panel voted no, July 2026

what.text: Emideltide is the international nonproprietary name listed by WHO for delta sleep-inducing peptide (DSIP). FDA notes it has no US adopted name (USAN). It is a chain of nine amino acids: Trp-Ala-Gly-Gly-Asp-Ala-Ser-Gly-Glu. It was first found in the blood of rabbits in 1963 and made in the lab in 1976. It is sold as a free base or as an acetate salt, which FDA treats as different substances.

src.label: FDA briefing document, emideltide (memo dated May 11, 2026), PCAC July 2026

what.text: The name comes from animal studies. Given to rabbits, rats and cats, it increased the slow "delta" brain waves of deep sleep. FDA's review says its sleep effects in animals seem to work through the body's opioid system: it does not bind opioid receptors directly, but it can trigger the release of endorphins.

src.label: FDA briefing document, emideltide (memo dated May 11, 2026), PCAC July 2026

what.text: In people, it is cleared from the blood very fast, with a half-life of about 8 minutes. FDA found no data on how it behaves when injected under the skin, the route it was nominated for in compounding.

src.label: FDA briefing document, emideltide (memo dated May 11, 2026), PCAC July 2026

what.text: Emideltide is not an approved medicine in the US or any country FDA searched. Using it for sleep is not an approved use anywhere.

research.text: Emideltide has been tested in people, but only in small studies from 1981 to 1998, all with injections into a vein. The early studies by one research group reported better sleep. Two double-blind studies by other research groups, in 1987 and 1992, found little or no benefit. No trial is registered on ClinicalTrials.gov.
Each study is listed below as it was run.

research.title: Six adults with insomnia, 1981

facts.v: double-blind, placebo-controlled crossover. Each person got DSIP or placebo by vein just before bed, on three test nights.
6 middle-aged adults with chronic insomnia
3 test nights
sleep recordings, sleepiness ratings, diaries

research.found: Sleep was longer, with fewer interruptions, from the second hour after the injection. In the first hour there was a slight arousing effect. No daytime sedation was reported. FDA noted the study was very small and did not report placebo numbers in full.

src.label: Schneider-Helmert and Schoenenberger, Experientia, 1981
FDA briefing document, emideltide (memo dated May 11, 2026), PCAC July 2026

research.title: Middle-aged and older adults, 1986

facts.v: placebo baseline nights, then DSIP by vein each evening, compared with outside healthy controls. No placebo group.
18 adults with chronic insomnia: 9 aged 29–59, 9 aged 60–83
one week of DSIP (6 doses), then one week of follow-up
time to fall asleep, time awake, total sleep, sleep efficiency

research.found: The author reported sleep improved to normal levels in both age groups. FDA said the small size and the lack of a proper control group limit what this shows.

src.label: Schneider-Helmert, Eur Neurol, 1986
FDA briefing document, emideltide (memo dated May 11, 2026), PCAC July 2026

research.title: Sleep and daytime performance, 1987

facts.v: seven nights of DSIP by vein, with placebo on the first and last nights. Results were compared with each person's baseline and with healthy people from outside the study.
14 middle-aged adults with chronic insomnia
7 nights of DSIP, with a placebo night at the start and at the end
sleep recordings, daytime tests, mood scales

research.found: Average time to fall asleep went from 58 to 28 minutes and total sleep from 313 to 385 minutes. The author called it placebo-controlled, but FDA said there was no placebo group, so the results are hard to interpret.

src.label: Schneider-Helmert, Eur Neurol, 1987
FDA briefing document, emideltide (memo dated May 11, 2026), PCAC July 2026

research.title: Six adults with severe insomnia, 1987

facts.v: double-blind, placebo-controlled crossover, done twice with a 4-day break
6 adults with severe chronic insomnia
9 nights per round; 4 nights of DSIP or placebo
sleep recordings, sleep quality ratings

research.found: Total sleep rose by about 20 minutes, but there were no significant differences from baseline or placebo. The authors concluded the sleep improvement was of little clinical significance.

src.label: Monti et al., Int J Clin Pharmacol Res, 1987
FDA briefing document, emideltide (memo dated May 11, 2026), PCAC July 2026

research.title: Sixteen adults with insomnia, 1992

facts.v: double-blind, matched pairs. Half got DSIP by vein and half got a glucose placebo, in the afternoon before three nights.
16 adults with chronic insomnia
5 nights in a sleep lab
sleep recordings, sleep quality, tiredness

research.found: Small differences in sleep efficiency and time to fall asleep were weak and may have come from a change in the placebo group. Subjective sleep quality did not change. The authors concluded short-term DSIP is not likely to be of major benefit for chronic insomnia.

src.label: Bes et al., Neuropsychobiology, 1992
FDA briefing document, emideltide (memo dated May 11, 2026), PCAC July 2026

items.text: an open study of 7 people with severe insomnia, given 10 injections. The author reported sleep was normal in all but one for 3 to 7 months afterwards. There was no control group.

src.label: Kaeser, Eur Neurol, 1984

items.text: FDA notes a 1986 review of these studies concluded the results were preliminary and did not show that DSIP reliably starts or keeps sleep.

src.label: FDA briefing document, emideltide (memo dated May 11, 2026), PCAC July 2026

research.title: First study in people, 1981

facts.v: double-blind crossover; DSIP or placebo slowly by vein in the morning
6 healthy volunteers (4 men, 2 women)
2 test days
sleep in the 130 minutes after the infusion, the next night's sleep, mood and alertness tests

research.found: Sleep in the 130 minutes after DSIP was 59% longer than after placebo (median). The next night, people fell asleep faster. No sedation, mood change or side effects were seen.

src.label: Schneider-Helmert et al., Int J Clin Pharmacol Ther Toxicol, 1981
FDA briefing document, emideltide (memo dated May 11, 2026), PCAC July 2026

research.text: One case report, 1984: a 35-year-old man with narcolepsy had a week of evening and a week of morning DSIP injections. Sleep attacks fell from 6 in the baseline week to 3 in each treatment week. A single case cannot show whether it works.

research.meta: Switzerland · 1984 · Open study, no control group
research.title: Withdrawal in hospital inpatients, 1984

facts.v: open-label, no comparison group; DSIP by vein when withdrawal symptoms appeared
107 inpatients: 60 withdrawing from opioids, 47 from alcohol
up to 6 days
withdrawal signs judged by doctors and nurses

research.found: The authors reported symptoms cleared or improved in most patients who could be evaluated, but anxiety eased slowly and some had anxiety and marked insomnia 1 to 3 days after stopping. FDA said the lack of blinding and a control group limits what this shows.

src.label: Dick et al., Eur Neurol, 1984
FDA briefing document, emideltide (memo dated May 11, 2026), PCAC July 2026

research.text: 1998: an open study of 7 people withdrawing from opioids. Symptom scores fell after the first injection, but only 2 people finished the full course, and both needed another drug for insomnia.

src.label: Backmund et al., J Clin Psychopharmacol, 1998
FDA briefing document, emideltide (memo dated May 11, 2026), PCAC July 2026

research.text: In rabbits, rats and cats, DSIP given into the brain or by injection increased deep-sleep brain waves, although results on sleep stages were not consistent. FDA found no standard toxicity studies (repeat-dose, cancer or reproduction) and no studies of whether it can be addictive.

items.text: FDA's scientists, in a review dated May 11, 2026, recommended against adding emideltide (free base or acetate) to the list of substances pharmacies may compound. They reviewed it for injection under the skin for opioid withdrawal, chronic insomnia and narcolepsy.

src.label: FDA briefing document, emideltide (memo dated May 11, 2026), PCAC July 2026

items.text: FDA found the substance is not well characterized, the human studies are small and poorly controlled, and there are no safety data for injection under the skin. It noted FDA-approved drugs exist for insomnia, narcolepsy and opioid withdrawal.

items.text: FDA's page of substances that may pose significant safety risks lists emideltide (DSIP) among nominations that were withdrawn after being in Category 2. FDA says compounded emideltide "may pose risk for immunogenicity for certain routes of administration" and that "the agency lacks sufficient information to know whether the drug would cause harm if administered to humans."

items.text: no outsourcing facility reported making emideltide products to FDA. after.text: Emideltide (DSIP) is not named on the WADA Prohibited List for 2026 or 2027. WADA class S0 bans at all times any pharmacological substance not covered by another class and with no current approval by any government health authority for human therapeutic use. For 2027, WADA adds "peptides" to the examples in S0. FDA found emideltide is not a registered drug in any country it searched. The lists do not say whether emideltide falls under S0.

side.text: Side effects are poorly known. FDA counts 209 people who had emideltide by vein in published studies, for 1 to 15 days. No one has published safety data for injection under the skin, the route nominated for compounding.

items.text: FDA says the small studies by vein reported it was well tolerated, with no significant adverse events. One study saw a slight arousing effect in the first hour.

Schneider-Helmert and Schoenenberger, Experientia, 1981

items.text: of 107 patients, 9 had minor, short-lived effects such as sweating, headache, nausea and dizziness. Three had serious reactions: two had low blood pressure at the start of the first injection, and one patient who got a second injection had "progressive" low blood pressure. Some patients had anxiety and marked insomnia 1 to 3 days after stopping.

unconfirmed: FDA has not posted the official vote record for the July 24, 2026 committee meeting; the vote counts come from Healio.
We found no FDA record of a final decision on emideltide after the July 2026 meeting.
The date emideltide was first placed in Category 2 is not shown on FDA's Category 2 page.
Status in the UK and Australia (TGA product register) was not checked against a regulator record.
Most published studies do not say whether they used the free base or the acetate form.
surprises: Emideltide is promoted for sleep, but the two double-blind insomnia studies by other research groups (1987 and 1992) found little or no benefit.
It was nominated for compounding as an injection under the skin, yet every published human study FDA found gave it into a vein, and FDA found no safety data for the under-the-skin route.
Of the seven peptides FDA's advisory committee reviewed in July 2026, emideltide was the only one the committee voted against (as reported by Healio).
